conversation_lines.text: Still really tired. And I feel shaky sometimes. The sadness is still there, but the voices are quieter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually progress. We’re also checking your thyroid because low thyroid can make depression worse. Your levels suggest mild hypothyroidism, so we’ll start a low dose of medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help my mood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially during pregnancy. We’ll monitor it closely. We also saw your white blood cell count is a bit high — could be from stress or mild inflammation. Nothing suggests infection right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a different treatment because your depression is severe and not improving fast enough with meds alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. It’s very effective for severe depression, especially in pregnancy. It’s safe when done carefully, and it can work faster than medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Isn’t that… shocking the brain? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But it’s done under anesthesia, so you’re asleep. A small, controlled current helps reset brain activity. Many patients feel much better after just a few sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it won’t hurt the baby?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We monitor the baby during the procedure. The risk is very low, and the benefit of treating your depression outweighs it. We do this often in pregnancy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’ll try it if it can help me feel like myself again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a brave decision. We’ll start with one session tomorrow. You’ll be asleep the whole time and wake up in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your anxiety today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nervous about the ECT. And I’ve been having heartburn again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you something for the heartburn — probably just reflux. And we’ll make sure you’re comfortable before ECT. You’ll have oxygen and monitoring the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. It shows mixed bacteria, but that’s likely from contamination during collection. No infection, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried it was a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. We’ll keep an eye on it, but you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re about to have your first ECT session. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I remember anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ll be fully asleep. You might feel groggy afterward, and some people have short-term memory blurs, but it usually clears up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, welcome back. The ECT went well. You had a good seizure response, which means the treatment reached the right areas. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired… and my muscles ache a little. But the heaviness in my chest feels lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. The aches are from the muscle relaxant. We’ll give you something for that. This is often the start of improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t hear the voices today. Not even once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. It may take a few more sessions, but you’re moving in the right direction. We’ll plan for another in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s your discharge day. Your mood is much improved, labs are stable, and you’re no longer having suicidal thoughts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel… not happy yet, but hopeful. And I’m not stiff or restless like I was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we wanted to hear. You’ll continue ECT as an outpatient, and your psychiatrist will adjust medications safely for pregnancy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my thyroid and anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and iron for anemia. Both are safe in pregnancy. Keep taking them and follow up with your OB.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma and reflux?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your inhaler as needed. For reflux, stick to small meals and avoid lying down after eating. We’ll send prescriptions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so scared when I came in. I feel like I can face this now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did an amazing job. Asking for help was the first step. Keep leaning on your care team. We’re here for you and your baby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to be healthy for my child.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will be. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over them, and you can leave once you’re packed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my family history. My mom had bipolar too. Does that mean my baby will?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a higher risk, but it’s not certain. What matters most is that you’re getting care now. That’s the best protection you can give your child.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thank you for not just treating my illness but listening to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re here for. Take care, and call if anything changes. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can breathe again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best outcome we could hope for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make my follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll also send a summary to your OB and therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Take care of yourself and your baby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your OB-GYN team members. I know you just got transferred from triage. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’m tired. My mind’s been racing. I haven’t been sleeping. I just… I don’t feel like myself since my dad passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry about your father. That’s a lot to carry, especially right now. We’ve read your history — you’ve been through a lot with your mood and ECT before. Is that what helped you last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. After the first session, I felt like a fog had lifted. But after Dad died, everything came back — the sadness, the voices… I couldn’t get out of bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve already spoken with the ECT team, and they’re planning to restart your treatments. We’ll do them here on Labor and Delivery so we can monitor the baby closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe for the baby? I keep worrying…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a really important question. The risk of untreated severe depression — for both you and the baby — is higher than the risk of ECT. We’ll monitor the fetal heart rate during each treatment, and if anything looks concerning, we’ll stop right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that helps. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your thyroid test came back. Your TSH is high — 9.5 — and your free T4 is low. That means you have hypothyroidism, which can make depression worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I had that. Could that be part of why I’ve felt so sluggish?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re starting you on levothyroxine today — 75 micrograms daily. It should help with your energy and mood over the next few weeks. We’ll check your levels again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. I just want to feel stable for my baby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling after yesterday’s ECT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little groggy still, but… I noticed something. The voices are quieter. Not gone, but not shouting anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. The fetal tracing was stable the whole time, so we’re on track for another session in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the baby’s okay. I’ve been so scared I wouldn’t be a good mom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing everything you can to take care of yourself — that’s the best thing you can do for your baby. We’re here to support you every step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two more ECT sessions. The psychiatry team says you’re responding well. How’s your mood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I cried yesterday — but it was just… sadness, not despair. I even called my mom. We talked about Dad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big step. Grieving with support is so important. Your blood pressure has been creeping up though — it was 148/92 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? I’ve been stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be pregnancy-induced hypertension. We’re watching it closely. If it gets worse, or if we see protein in your urine, it could be preeclampsia — and we might need to deliver sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I’m not due for another month. Is the baby ready?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At 36 weeks, babies do pretty well. We’d only deliver if it’s safer for you and the baby than continuing the pregnancy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is still high — 152/96 — and your urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is elevated. Uric acid is up too. We’re concerned about preeclampsia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… does that mean I’m going to deliver now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s the safest choice. We’ll start induction today with medication to soften the cervix, then Pitocin. It might take a while, but we’ll support you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m scared, but I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi — just checking in. You’ve been in labor for a few days now. Cervix is dilating slowly. Still holding strong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired… contractions are intense. But I’m doing my breathing. My boyfriend’s here — he’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’re increasing the Pitocin a bit to help things progress. Baby’s heart rate looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re fully dilated! Time to start pushing. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Congratulations — it’s a healthy baby girl! She’s crying strong, Apgar 8 and 9. You did amazing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s beautiful… I can’t believe it. I’m a mom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you are. We did have to do a manual extraction of the placenta — it was retained. But you’re stable, no hemorrhage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It happens sometimes, especially after a long labor. We’ve given you antibiotics just in case, since there’s a small risk of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sore, especially down there. But happy. I held her for 20 minutes yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. You had a second-degree tear — we repaired it. It’ll heal. Any fever or pain beyond the incision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just the usual soreness. I’m taking the ibuprofen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Urine culture came back — less than 10,000 organisms, so no infection. We’ll stop the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry stopped by. They’re really pleased with your mood. You’re clear, engaged — a big change from when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have sad moments, but I’m not trapped in it. I even laughed yesterday when the baby sneezed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s healing. They’re switching you from perphenazine to quetiapine — it’s safer long-term and helps with both mood and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need ECT after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, outpatient ECT weekly for now, then tapering. You’ll follow up with your psychiatrist regularly. This plan helped you before — it can again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had another ECT session. How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before — groggy for an hour, then fine. I’m glad I can keep doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your mood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still stable. I’m even thinking about the future — maybe going back to nursing someday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great goal. One step at a time. For now, focus on healing and bonding with your baby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Just a few things to go over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m nervous but ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking levothyroxine daily — same dose. Get your TSH checked in six weeks. And quetiapine at bedtime — it helps with mood and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the prenatal vitamins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep those too — especially important while breastfeeding. And ibuprofen or acetaminophen for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And ECT? When’s my first appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Next week, same day and time as today. Your psychiatrist will coordinate it. And you’ll see them in between for check-ins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you — for everything. I feel like I have a real chance now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do. You’ve worked so hard. Keep reaching out — to your team, your family, your faith. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick visit — your incision looks great, no signs of infection. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so ready to go home. My mom’s excited to meet the baby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come so far — from severe depression, through delivery, to this moment. I’m really proud of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Any questions before we go over the instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one — if I start feeling down again, what should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your psychiatrist right away. Don’t wait. And if you ever feel unsafe, go to the ER. You’re not failing — you’re being proactive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going home with a solid plan — meds, therapy, ECT, support. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. For listening. For not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Never. Take care of yourself — and that beautiful baby. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re officially going home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it. It’s been… a month, almost.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A tough month, but look how far you’ve come. You’re strong, and you’re not alone. Keep leaning on your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. And congratulations again — on becoming a mom, and on your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you in a few days to check in. Until then, rest, bond with your baby, and take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready for this next chapter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re here for it with you. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re all rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps more than you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with a headache and high blood pressure. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this headache since this morning. I tried ibuprofen and drinking water, but it hasn’t helped much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when you checked your blood pressure at home, what was it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My systolic was in the 160s. It felt high, so I came in right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. We just checked it again and it’s 183 over 104. That’s considered severe range, especially after delivery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve been feeling okay otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with a headache. We want to bring it down safely. You’ll get a medication through your IV called labetalol to help lower it quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I had high blood pressure before during pregnancy, but it went away after I delivered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were diagnosed with preeclampsia last time. Sometimes blood pressure can flare up again in the first week or two after delivery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this is related to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s called postpartum hypertension. We’re going to monitor you closely and start a pill to keep your pressure stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay in the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at least for a day or two. We want to make sure your blood pressure stays under control and your headache improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also sent some blood tests to check your liver and kidneys, just to be safe. These help us rule out something more serious like HELLP syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from my last admission. Everything came back normal then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same this time — your labs are normal. That’s reassuring. Your urine protein is slightly elevated, but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been worried about my baby too — am I safe to breastfeed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both labetalol and the new blood pressure pill, nifedipine, are safe for breastfeeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has come down to 158 over 92 after the IV meds. Still a bit high, but improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My headache is a little better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common — headaches often improve as the pressure comes down. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure overnight stayed in the 150s to 160s. We’re going to continue the nifedipine and check it every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that still too high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to see it below 140/90. You’re close. We’ll give it more time and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pressure is now 128 over 68 — that’s excellent. And your headache is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a little dull ache now, but it doesn’t bother me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep you on the nifedipine daily and send it home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also take Synthroid, Seroquel, and Zantac — should I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of those. You’re also being started on acyclovir — I see you have a history of herpes, and we want to prevent outbreaks postpartum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot to mention that. Is it safe with breastfeeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, acyclovir is considered safe. We’ll give you a prescription to finish the course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had stable pressures all night — all in the 120s over 60s. I think we can plan for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about my ECT appointment? It was scheduled for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with your psychiatrist. It’s safer to delay it by a week now that your blood pressure just stabilized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand. I don’t want to risk anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you a prescription for nifedipine for the next month, and you’ll follow up with your OB and primary doctor in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my blood pressure goes up again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep monitoring it. If it’s over 150/100 or you get a bad headache, vision changes, or chest pain, go straight to triage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just take it easy, keep up with your meds, and we’ll see you soon in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — should I be worried about this happening again in the future?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, especially with a history of preeclampsia. But we’ll monitor you closely in any future pregnancies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, continue your thyroid and psychiatric meds as prescribed. Your body’s adjusting on many levels right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. It’s a lot, but I feel supported.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Discharge papers are ready — nurse will go over instructions and your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself and your baby. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted last night with left lower abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. The pain started a few days after I restarted my birth control pills. It’s constant, crampy, and it radiates down my left leg. It feels just like my old endometriosis pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had endometriosis before—was it confirmed with surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice. Laparoscopy, biopsy-proven. After the second surgery, I was pain-free for a while. Pregnancy helped too. But now it feels like it’s back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned you restarted your birth control recently. Was that Apri?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a week ago. I thought it might help, but the pain started right after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Sometimes hormonal changes can trigger flares. Your heart rate has been high—around 130 when you came in. Are you feeling anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure. The pain is really intense. I’ve had worse, but I’m worried about taking strong painkillers because of my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve been sober since pregnancy, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I haven’t used anything since I found out I was pregnant. I’m on quetiapine and nifedipine, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep those going. We’ve given you IV fluids—3 liters—because your labs showed mild dehydration and low potassium. That might be contributing to the tachycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much. The pain makes me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you Phenergan for that. And we used ketorolac and some oxycodone in the ER, but you said it didn’t help much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. Morphine helped a little, but I don’t want to rely on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use it only if needed. We’ve also started you on a lidocaine patch for localized relief. And we’re continuing ibuprofen and acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. But what about the pain? Is it endometriosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve done a pelvic ultrasound and a CT scan. No signs of ovarian torsion, infection, or bowel issues like diverticulitis. The gynecology team reviewed it and agrees it’s not classic for an acute problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it could still be endometriosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The scans can’t rule it out completely. Given your history and the type of pain, it’s a strong possibility. But your gynecologist noted it’s not fully typical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want it under control. I can’t function like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted pain management. They suggest continuing the current plan and possibly adding duloxetine later through your psychiatrist, if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the blood I saw? Just a few drops, two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked. No hemorrhoids or fissures on exam. Hemoglobin is stable. It was likely minor and self-limited. We’ll follow up as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m just worried something’s being missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ve done a thorough workup. Nothing urgent shows up. The pain is real, and we’re treating it. Your heart rate has already come down to 110 with fluids and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. The lidocaine patch helps some.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the ibuprofen and acetaminophen on schedule. You can use tramadol for breakthrough pain, up to every four hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tramadol? I’ve used it before. It’s okay, not too strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s safer given your history. We’ll avoid stronger opioids unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re also on heparin injections to prevent clots, and senna with Colace to help with constipation from pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I haven’t had a bowel movement in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The stool softeners should help. Let the nurse know if you’re uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re looking more comfortable today. Pain improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely better. Still a dull ache, but I can walk without wincing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your heart rate is down to 90, and you’re eating more. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s good news. But what if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with tramadol, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen. Keep using the lidocaine patch. And stay on your birth control—your gyn says it’s still the best long-term option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it started the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might have triggered a flare, but stopping it could make things worse long-term. Your gyn will help you decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll follow up with her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call if the pain gets worse or you have fever, vomiting, or more bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re doing well—pain controlled, eating, and ambulating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send you home with prescriptions for tramadol, ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and the lidocaine patch. Keep taking your regular meds: Apri, levothyroxine, quetiapine, nifedipine, and ranitidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I have my follow-up with Dr. ___ next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. If the pain persists, they might consider other options, like adjusting your hormonal therapy or revisiting duloxetine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep track of it and let them know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re cleared to go home. Take it easy, stay hydrated, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your time and care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and I hope you feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your rectal bleeding was minor and likely not serious, but mention it at your follow-up just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We’ll see you out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You came in last night after taking some tramadol and Phenergan. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I took more than I should have. I was arguing with my mom, and I just couldn’t handle it. I wanted it to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. It takes a lot of courage to come in. Were you planning to hurt yourself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I didn’t want to live anymore. I’ve been so overwhelmed—my pain, my mom needing me, everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for being honest. We’re going to keep you safe here. You had a brief episode of low oxygen and were given Narcan. You responded well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember waking up in the ER, confused. I didn’t think I’d need that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tramadol in high doses can suppress breathing. We’re monitoring you closely. No signs of serotonin syndrome or heart issues, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on tramadol for my endometriosis pain. It’s the only thing that helps sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But because of the overdose, we’re stopping tramadol for now. Psychiatry is adjusting your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain? It’s been really bad lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage it with the lidocaine patch and other non-opioid options. Your gynecology team can help long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I guess I just feel stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. We’re here to support you. A CT scan of your head was normal—no bleeding or stroke. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about brain damage or something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. Your labs are improving—kidney function, electrolytes, all looking stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had liver issues before from past drug use, but I’ve been clean since pregnancy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are normal now. That’s great. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still sad, but not as foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your vitals are stable. Psychiatry lowered your Seroquel to 150mg at night and added a PRN dose for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 300mg. Will that make me more anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re adjusting it carefully. The lower dose may help with side effects, and you can take the PRN if you feel overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to spiral again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preventing that. You’re medically stable, and you’ll be transferred to inpatient psychiatry for ECT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: ECT again? It helped before, but I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a strong option for treatment-resistant depression. The team will go over the risks and benefits with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember memory fog afterward, but I felt better for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The goal is to help you regain stability. You’ll be medically cleared for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my thyroid and acid reflux? I’m on levothyroxine and ranitidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep both. Your thyroid levels are stable, and ranitidine helps with stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want other things flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. Your labs are excellent—better than admission. You’re cleared for transfer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous but ready, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. You’ll go to extended psychiatric care. They’ll start ECT soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to stop eating tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nothing after midnight the night before your first ECT. The team will confirm the schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? What do I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue levothyroxine, ranitidine, prenatal vitamins, lidocaine patch, and the Depo shot. Seroquel is now 150mg at night, plus PRN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No tramadol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. It’s too risky given your history. We’ll work with pain management later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. You’ve already taken the hardest step—asking for help. We’re all rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. For listening, I mean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care. The transport team will be here soon to take you to psychiatry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll miss my baby. I hope I can get back to her soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Focus on healing now. The stronger you get, the sooner you’ll be back with her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I’m fighting for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then keep going. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all anyone can ask. Take it one step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team while you're here. Can I sit down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I guess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you came in after having some thoughts about driving into a tree. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was driving, and suddenly I just felt so heavy. I thought… maybe if I didn’t stop, it would all end. But I did stop. I called my psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I'm really glad you did. That took courage. You're not alone in this. We're going to keep you safe while you're here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to hurt myself. But sometimes the depression just… takes over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You’ve been through a lot. I see you’ve been on ECT before and it’s helped. Psychiatry is setting that up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it helps. But my veins are terrible. They always have trouble starting IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually why we’re planning a port-a-cath. It’s a small device placed under the skin that makes it easier to give treatments like ECT without poking your veins each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a common procedure. It’s done under local anesthesia, and we’ll make sure you’re comfortable. It’s scheduled for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. That sounds better than getting stuck every time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We also started you on lithium last night—150 mg at bedtime. Psychiatry wants to increase it to help stabilize your mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken lithium before. Does it have side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel a little shaky or thirsty at first. We’ll check your levels and kidney function regularly to keep it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll watch for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night look stable. White blood cell count is normal, thyroid is fine. We’re still waiting on the lithium level to confirm it’s in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the methadone in my urine test a problem? I haven’t taken any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. The test did show methadone, but you’re not on it. We’ll document that you deny use. It could be a false positive or contamination, but we’ll keep it on record.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want anyone thinking I’m using drugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Your history shows you’ve been sober since pregnancy. We trust your word and will note that clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a heads-up—the port-a-cath procedure is set for noon. You’ll be given medication to relax, and the team will place it in your chest. It’ll be covered with a dressing after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel some pressure, but not sharp pain. The area will be numbed. Afterward, there might be some soreness, like after any minor surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m nervous, but I want this to work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The port-a-cath was placed successfully. The X-ray shows the line is in the right spot, near your heart. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it… inside my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tip is in a large vein near the heart—perfect for safe delivery of medications. It’s not in the heart muscle. You’ll barely notice it once healed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the site feeling? Any redness or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little tender, but not bad. I can move my arm okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s normal. We’ll keep the dressing dry and change it in a couple of days. No lifting more than 10 pounds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, psychiatry wants to increase your lithium to 300 mg at bedtime. We’ll check your level again tomorrow to make sure it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your lithium level came back at 0.3, which is a bit low. That’s why we increased the dose. It may take a few days to rise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it help with the suicidal thoughts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help stabilize your mood over time. Combined with ECT, it gives you the best chance to feel better. You’re not on this alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood count is improving—hemoglobin up from 11.2 to 12.2. That’s good. Everything else looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the B12 deficiency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You’re on a multivitamin now, which includes B12. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatric team saw you this morning. They said your mood is more stable, and you’re denying current suicidal thoughts. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel down, but not like last week. I think the ECT will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your first ECT session for Friday. You’ll be asleep during it, and you’ll wake up in recovery. Most people feel tired afterward, but not in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from before. I just hope it works again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your port site is healing well—just mild swelling and tenderness. No signs of infection. You can start gentle arm movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’re here to support you through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big day tomorrow—your first ECT. You’ll be taken to the procedure room, given anesthesia, and it’ll be over in minutes. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I remember anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ll be fully asleep. Some people have short-term memory gaps, but it usually improves. The team will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You did great with ECT today. You woke up alert, and your vitals are stable. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. A little confused, but it’s clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. You’ll rest here for a bit, then we’ll get you ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being transferred to Deaconess 4, an inpatient psychiatric unit, for continued ECT and care. You’ll stay there for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m a little nervous, but I know I need this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay to feel that way. You’ve made real progress. You’re safer, your mood is more stable, and you’re taking steps toward healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. For listening. For not judging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re doing hard work, and we’re proud of you. Keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Your mom will be here soon to go with you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in after talking about a difficult moment during your ECT appointment. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… yesterday I was driving to get coffee. Out of nowhere, I just felt this urge to end it. I pressed the gas all the way down and left it for about a minute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really overwhelming. Did you think about crashing the car?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought about it… but I didn’t turn the wheel. I just let go of the gas and kept driving. I don’t know why I didn’t do it. I didn’t want to die, but I didn’t care if I lived either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for sharing that. It takes courage. You’re not alone in this. We’re going to keep you safe here while we figure out the next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel like everyone would be better off without me. My mom, my boyfriend, my brother… I’m a burden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that pain. But your life matters. We’re going to work on helping you feel that again. For now, we’ll have someone check in with you regularly to make sure you’re safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. I kept thinking about my baby. I’m scared I’m not a good mom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Being a new mom is hard, especially with everything else you’re managing. You’ve been through a lot—bipolar disorder, chronic pain, endometriosis. That’s not easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s exhausting. And I used to take ECT weekly. It helped, but I’ve missed a few sessions because of everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart ECT while you’re here. It’s often very effective for treatment-resistant depression. We’ve scheduled your first session for Thursday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m nervous. Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re asleep during the treatment, so you don’t feel anything. Some people have a headache or muscle soreness afterward, but we’ll manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… if it helps, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still tired. My stomach hurts—probably from the endometriosis. And I’ve been heartburn a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can adjust your meds for the reflux. And we’ll keep monitoring your pain. You’re on thyroid medication too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, levothyroxine. I take it every morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll make sure that continues. Your labs look stable, so no changes needed there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after your first ECT session?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. My head hurts a little, and I feel confused. Did I say anything weird?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Some short-term confusion and headache are common. You didn’t say anything unusual. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember much after they put the mask on. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, that’s expected. Most people don’t remember the procedure. We’ll keep monitoring your memory, but this is typical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mood seems a bit brighter today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t know… maybe a little less heavy? I still feel guilty about being a burden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That guilt is part of the illness. You’re not a burden. We’re here to support you, not because you’re failing, but because you’re fighting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… that helps to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your next ECT for Monday. How’s the headache been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Just a dull ache now. I’m scared of losing more memories though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using bilateral stimulation, which is effective but can affect memory. We’ll keep the dose as low as possible to help protect that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just don’t want to forget my baby’s first year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll document your concerns and review them with the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after today’s ECT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Less confused than last time. I think I’m starting to adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your mood is improving too. You smiled at the nurse today—small things matter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even notice. Maybe I’m not completely numb anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking ahead to discharge. How do you feel about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. What if I have another episode like the driving one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s valid. But you’re not alone. You’ll continue ECT weekly at the outpatient center. And you have a strong support system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My boyfriend’s been great. And my mom helps with the baby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll also set you up with therapy focused on borderline personality traits and coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your thyroid levels are stable. Any more stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but the meds help. I’ve been using my inhaler too—my chest gets tight sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep using it as prescribed. Asthma can flare with stress, so managing your mood helps your breathing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow’s your last day. You’ll have one more ECT before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about leaving. What if I start feeling that way again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a crisis plan. If thoughts come back, you call your therapist, go to the ED, or call 988. You don’t have to handle it alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that helps. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This stay was about stabilization. Now it’s about maintenance. You’ve made real progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Ready for your final ECT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: As ready as I’ll ever be. I’m glad I did this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. You’ve worked hard. After the treatment, we’ll go over your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well today. How’s your head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little sore. Nothing like the first time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Now, for discharge: you’ll continue weekly ECT, see your psychiatrist every two weeks, and start dialectical behavior therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: DBT? I’ve heard it helps with emotional control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s especially helpful for borderline personality traits and managing intense emotions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to be present for my baby. I don’t want to miss moments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. This is the beginning of that. Keep reaching out. You’re not a burden—you’re someone worth fighting for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Never. Take care of yourself. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your allergies are flagged: Reglan, Erythromycin, Effexor, Haldol, Invega. Avoid those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll tell any new doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. Your ride is here. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One day at a time. I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember, progress isn’t linear. If you stumble, reach out. That’s strength, not weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve already shown so much strength. Keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re proud of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s true. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lin, one of the psychiatry residents. I’m here to talk with you about what happened tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just… I threw a table. I don’t know why. I was at home and everything felt too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can you tell me what ‘too much’ felt like? Were you upset, angry, overwhelmed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both. Angry and scared. Like I couldn’t breathe. My chest was tight. I felt like I was disappearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really intense. Have you felt that way before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. A few times. Last month, I drove too fast on the highway. But I didn’t want to crash. I just wanted to feel something real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from your last admission. You were doing ECT then, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I was. But I stopped after I got out. I thought I was okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common for symptoms to come back if treatment is interrupted, especially with bipolar and borderline personality disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just… I don’t want to keep doing this. Breaking things. Feeling like I’m not here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to help you stabilize. You’re safe here. We’ll start by adjusting your medications and getting you back into therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your chart. You’re on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism—still taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I have it at home. I’ve been skipping it sometimes. I forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thyroid levels can affect your mood and energy. We’ll make sure you get it daily while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my endometriosis pain—it’s been worse lately. I’ve been using ibuprofen, but it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Chronic pain can make emotional regulation harder. We’ll manage it carefully—avoiding opioids since there’s a history of abuse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I shouldn’t use them. But when the pain hits, I just want it gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll work on non-opioid strategies and explore what triggers the flare-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your meds. We’re restarting lamotrigine for bipolar and adding naltrexone to help with cravings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Naltrexone? For alcohol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You mentioned drinking a few times a week to cope. Naltrexone can reduce the urge and help you stay in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be dependent on anything. Not pills, not alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This isn’t about dependence. It’s about support. Like using a cane when your leg is weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess… I can try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little calmer. Still sad sometimes. But I didn’t have that ‘disappearing’ feeling yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re also going to restart ECT twice a week. It helped before—let’s see if it helps now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of it. The memory loss…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use the lowest effective dose. Most people notice improvement in mood without major memory issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. If it helps me feel real again, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had your first ECT yesterday. How did you feel afterward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. A little confused for a few hours. But this morning, I cried when I saw a photo of my cat. I haven’t felt anything like that in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Feeling emotions again means the numbness is lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to go back to feeling nothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re building a plan to prevent that—meds, ECT, and therapy. DBT starts tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How was the first DBT group?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: We talked about distress tolerance. I liked the idea of ‘surfing the wave’ instead of reacting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Emotions rise and fall. You don’t have to act on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But what if I can’t stop myself? Like with the table?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what the skills are for. And we’ll keep your meds optimized. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two ECT sessions. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My head hurts a little after, but Tylenol helps. And I’m remembering things—like what I ate, what we talked about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That means your cognition is stable. Your mood reports are improving too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have days where I feel empty. But not every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Recovery isn’t linear. The fact that you’re noticing the difference is progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re halfway through your stay. Discharge planning has started. How do you feel about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. What if I fall apart again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have support. Weekly ECT for now, DBT group, and your psychiatrist will see you every two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel like I’m losing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You call your crisis line, go to the ER, or come back here. Your safety plan will list all the steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Thyroid levels are stable. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that wasn’t making me worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. But staying on it helps prevent mood swings. We’ll keep you on the same dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try not to skip it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow is your last ECT session here. After discharge, it will continue outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going off-site for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange transportation. And you’ll have a contact person at the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I don’t want to lose the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day. You’ve done really well. Mood more stable, engaging in therapy, no self-harm thoughts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have hard moments. But I’m using the skills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what matters. Keep using them. Here’s your discharge packet—meds, appointments, crisis plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I need to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can always come back. This isn’t failure. It’s part of recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. For not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re a team. Take care of yourself. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in because of fevers. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had fevers up to 102 for about nine days. My PCP thought it was cellulitis in my second toe and gave me Keflex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how’s the toe now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. But now my fourth toe is hurting more, and the fevers came back after a short break.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also noticed your left chest port was a little tender. Any pain or redness there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little sore, but no redness or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned that the port might be infected. Your blood work shows a high white count, and we’ve started you on IV fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So the port could be causing the fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a possibility. We’ll wait for blood cultures to confirm, but if it’s infected, we may need to remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially if the infection spreads. But we’re catching it early. You’re already on vancomycin, which covers common bacteria like staph.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my diarrhea? Started after the Keflex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested for C. diff. It came back negative, so it’s likely just a side effect. We’ll keep you on Imodium for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures grew MSSA — that’s a type of staph bacteria. It’s likely coming from your port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MSSA? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we’re on top of it. The plan is to remove the port today to stop the source of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? How long will it take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a quick procedure under local anesthesia. You’ll feel some pressure, but not sharp pain. Surgeons will do it this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port was successfully removed. No signs of pus or severe infection around it. We’ll send it for culture to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue IV antibiotics. Once we confirm the bacteria are cleared, we’ll switch you to a PICC line for outpatient treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are still pending, but you’re looking better — fevers are gone, and your heart rate is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My toe pain is also better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no signs of cellulitis now. We think the initial Keflex helped that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line in your right arm today so you can finish antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Any risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low risk. We’ll use ultrasound to guide it. Main risks are bleeding or infection, but we take precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: PICC line is in place. Chest X-ray confirms it’s positioned correctly in the superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need two sets of negative blood cultures first. Then you’ll finish a two-week course of IV nafcillin through the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All blood cultures since yesterday are negative. That’s a great sign — the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We also did an echocardiogram to check your heart — no signs of infection there, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. Thanks for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable. We’re transitioning you from vancomycin to IV nafcillin — it’s better for MSSA and easier on the kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rarely, it can cause rash or diarrhea. We’ll monitor your labs daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative again. The diarrhea is likely from the antibiotics, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I stop the Imodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if the diarrhea improves. We don’t want you getting dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day — your last set of cultures is negative. You’re ready for discharge planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to an extended care facility. They’ll manage your IV antibiotics and monitor the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About two weeks, until you finish the nafcillin. Then the PICC will be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just reviewing your discharge plan. You’ll continue all your regular meds — aripiprazole, bupropion, tramadol, and the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been taking them regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Loperamide to take as needed for diarrhea. And you’ll get daily IV nafcillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any restrictions at the facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the PICC site clean and dry. Don’t lift heavy things with that arm. Report any redness, swelling, or fever immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my mental health? I’ve been feeling okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable — no mood changes, no SI. Keep in touch with your psychiatrist and therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m seeing Dr. ___ for ECT too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ve communicated with them. Continue as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s discharge day. You look great — pink cheeks, alert, no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had MSSA bacteremia from your chest port, which caused sepsis. We removed the port, treated you with antibiotics, and you’ve responded well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The blood is clear. You just need to finish the course to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you — for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The team will send your records to the facility. Call us if anything changes before your PICC removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to get back to my mom’s and see my daughter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a good plan. Take care, and good luck with recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over discharge instructions one more time before you leave.
